passages.where: The Teacher tells the young to remember their Creator before the days come of which they will say, I find no pleasure in them. Then he describes old age in a haunting poem of a house falling quiet: the keepers of the house tremble, the strong men stoop, the grinders cease because they are few, those at the windows see dimly. Scripture names the body's decline honestly, without flattery and without contempt.

An old believer who has trusted God since birth prays, do not discard me in my old age, do not forsake me when my strength fails. His enemies say God has left him because he is weak. The fear of being set aside when one is no longer strong is old, and Scripture lets the aging pray it out loud.

The gods of Babylon are statues that have to be loaded onto weary animals and carried. Israel's God says the opposite: I have carried you from the womb, and even to your old age and gray hairs I will carry you. A failing body does not make a person a burden to God; he has been the one carrying all along.

A song for the Sabbath pictures the righteous as palm trees and cedars planted in God's house, still bearing fruit in old age, healthy and green. The fruit it names is a voice: to proclaim that the LORD is upright. Old age in Scripture is a season of bearing fruit, not only of losing strength.

Gray hair is called a crown of glory, found along the path of righteousness. In a culture that hides every sign of age, Proverbs treats it as honor. The crown is the life lived to reach it, not the years alone.

Young Elihu waited to speak out of respect for age, thinking many years should teach wisdom. Then he says that understanding comes from the breath of the Almighty, and it is not only the old who are wise. Scripture honors age without pretending that years make anyone wise automatically. Wisdom in old age is still a gift and a choice.

David invites Barzillai, who had fed the king in his exile, to live at court in Jerusalem. Barzillai, eighty years old, declines with honesty: he can no longer taste what he eats or hear the singers, and he would be a burden. He asks to die in his own town near his parents' grave and sends a younger man in his place. Aging well can include knowing what to hand on.

In the chapter that also commands love of neighbor, Israel is told to rise in the presence of the elderly and honor the aged, and the command ends with fear your God, I am the LORD. Honor for the old is tied directly to reverence for God, not left to custom or sentiment.

Paul tells Titus what to teach older men and older women: steadiness, self-control, sound faith, love and endurance, and for older women a role as teachers of good. The church is not to retire its elders. It expects them to teach, by word and by the shape of their lives.

Simeon, righteous and devout, has spent his life waiting for God's promised comfort for Israel. When he takes the infant Jesus in his arms, he says God may now dismiss his servant in peace, for his eyes have seen God's salvation. An old man's long waiting ends not in bitterness but in praise.

The women of Bethlehem bless the LORD over Naomi's newborn grandson: he will renew her life and sustain her in her old age. Naomi, who came home empty and bitter, is given a future through a daughter-in-law who loves her. God's care for the aged often comes through the next generation.

whole: Aging arrives slowly and then all at once. The body does less than it did, the doctor's visits multiply, names come more slowly, friends begin to die, and the world seems to be built for people who are younger and faster. Some feel set aside after retirement, unsure what they are for. Some fear dependence more than death. Many live in a culture that sells youth and treats age as a problem to be hidden, and they have absorbed more of that than they realize. Christians are not exempt, and church life can quietly favor the young as well.

Scripture neither flatters age nor despises it. Ecclesiastes describes the failing body more vividly than any medical chart: trembling hands, stooping backs, dimming eyes, the sound of the mill fading. Barzillai admits he can no longer taste his food or hear the singers. The psalmist fears being discarded when his strength fails. Yet the same Bible calls gray hair a crown of glory, commands Israel to stand up when the old enter, and pictures the righteous bearing fruit in old age. It holds the decline and the dignity together, and it roots the dignity not in what the body can still do but in the God who has carried a person from birth and promises to carry them to gray hairs.

That shapes the wisdom of growing old. It means accepting limits honestly, as Barzillai did, and handing on what you can no longer carry. It means continuing to bear fruit in the ways that remain: prayer, teaching, encouragement, telling the next generation what God has done, which the psalmist asks to live long enough to do. It means letting age make you wiser rather than only older, since Elihu was right that years alone do not make anyone wise. It means receiving care without shame when the time comes. And it means the church honoring its elders in fact, by listening to them, giving them work, and visiting them, rather than simply making room for them at the edges.

The hope Scripture offers the aging is not that the body will last, but that God will. He carried Israel from the womb and promised to carry them still in old age. Simeon spent a lifetime waiting and was not disappointed. For those in Christ, the outer self may waste away while the inner self is renewed, and the last chapter is resurrection, not decline. Old age is not a waiting room at the edge of a life. It can be the season when a life is most clearly seen to have been held by God all along.
sit: What is one thing God has done in your life that the next generation has not yet heard from you, and who could you tell?

prayer.lead: An old believer asks God not to leave him until he has told the next generation what God has done. Pray it at whatever age you are.
